passage: Transcript, morning handover, Thornfield Riding School, staff room. Manager Ellery: Handover, quickly, the nine o'clock hack is tacking up. Horses first. Bramble saw the farrier yesterday, new shoes all round, he is fine for work. Duchess is on box rest, day three of seven, the leg is cooler but the vet said seven and we do seven, so she comes off the lesson board through Sunday. Whoever mucks her out, she has learned to open the new bolt, so the clip goes on, every time, I mean it. Petra: She opened it twice yesterday. Once with a pony watching, which is how it spreads. Ellery: Exactly. Clips on both stables in that row, then. The grey pony, Mistral, is trialing the new bit in the 11 o'clock lesson only, and I want whoever teaches it to write two honest sentences on the card after, not the word fine. Next, people. The 2 p.m. beginner class has a new child, Oskar, seven years old, whose form says asthma, inhaler in a green bag, and the bag stays on the gate post, not in the office, while he rides. Petra: Which pony for him? Ellery: Biscuit. Small child, steady pony, no experiments on day one. Last thing: the hay delivery slides to Thursday, so we open the reserve stack this afternoon, and the reserve is the older cut, so shake it out well and any bale that smells wrong comes to me, not into a net. Questions? Go. The nine o'clock is waiting.
question: How many days of box rest does Duchess have in total?

passage: Verbatim record, Ostgate Museum acquisitions meeting, item two. Curator Fallon: The offer is the Merrivale collection: 61 pieces of local pottery, 1820 to 1900, from the kiln sites along the Ost. The family asks 15,000 dollars, and the independent valuation came back at 19,500, so the price is fair to generous. Registrar Chen: Provenance? Fallon: Documented for 54 pieces, bills of sale and the kiln ledgers. Seven pieces have gaps, and two of those seven match descriptions in the 1968 theft report from the Delft House museum. Chen: Then we cannot touch those two. Fallon: Agreed, and the family, told this, withdrew them from the offer without argument, which I found reassuring rather than the opposite. The price drops to 14,200 for 59 pieces. Director Musa: Storage. The ceramics store is at 91 percent. Where do 59 pieces live? Chen: We deaccessioned the duplicate agricultural tools in the spring precisely to clear shelving. The space exists as of last month. Musa: Conservation costs? Fallon: Eleven pieces need work, mostly old rivet repairs to redo, estimated 3,000 over two years, and the Fenwick Trust's ceramics fund is open for exactly this in October. Musa: Then I hear a total ask of 14,200 now, 3,000 contingent later, for the defining local collection we will not see offered again. Board approval threshold is 10,000, so this goes to the board, with this committee's recommendation. In favor of recommending? Three. Against? None. Chen drafts the provenance annex, and the two withdrawn pieces get a letter to Delft House either way; they should know where their pots are.
question: What price does the family ask for the 59 pieces after the withdrawal?

passage: Transcript, town of Bellwether traffic working group, the school corner. Chair Lindt: Everyone has walked the corner this month, per our agreement. Observations. Reyes: I stood there Tuesday morning. The crossing guard, Mrs. Pinsky, is the entire system. Cars stop for her that would not stop for a sign. The danger window is 8:12 to 8:25, when the two buses and the parents' cars arrive together. Okafor: I counted Thursday: 34 cars turning left across the crossing in that window, eleven of them faster than they should. And the sight line to the left is the hedge at number 12, which is the town's own hedge, on town land. Chair Lindt: The hedge is ours? Okafor: Ours. I checked the plat at the office. We have been debating mirrors and beacons for a year, and the cheapest fix has been the town's own shrubbery. Reyes: Cutting the hedge costs a morning. The beacon quote was 7,000 dollars. Chair Lindt: We can do both, but the order matters: hedge this week, then measure again. If the sight line fixes the worst of it, the beacon money can go to the sidewalk gap on Fenn Street, which this group promised two years running. Okafor: Motion: hedge cut to fence height by parks crew this week, Okafor repeats the count in two weeks same day and window, decision on the beacon deferred until that count is in hand. Reyes: Second. Chair Lindt: Carried, three to nil. And someone thank Mrs. Pinsky formally; the minutes should say the corner works because she does.
question: During what time window do the buses and parents' cars arrive together?

passage: Minutes, verbatim by vote of the body, Duncraig Curling Club special meeting on the ice plant. President Nairn: The compressor. Sandy has the report. Ice Manager Sandy Weir: Plainly: she is dying. The engineer gives the old girl one season, maybe two, and parts are scavenge only since the maker folded. Replacement, installed, 118,000 dollars. The club's capital fund holds 61,000. President Nairn: Options. Weir: Three. Borrow the difference, and the bank's terms are workable, I have a letter. Merge ice with the Aldbrae club, who have capacity and have asked before, which halves our costs and, say it honestly, halves our club. Or the third, from the members' suggestion box, in Etta Cormack's handwriting though unsigned: sell the beer license story properly, run the summer bonspiel as a real fundraiser, and ask the 214 members for 200 dollars each, which raises 42,800 and closes most of the gap with the borrowing small. Fraser: People will balk at 200. Cormack, from the floor: Then they can balk at driving forty minutes to Aldbrae in January. I signed nothing because handwriting should be enough among curlers. Laughter. President Nairn: Straw poll before the formal motion: borrow all of it, hands? Six. Merge? Two. The Cormack plan, levy plus small loan? Thirty-one. The formal motion will be drafted from the third option, vote by post per the constitution, papers out within two weeks. And the minutes will record that the compressor has been called the old girl since 1974, and that she is owed a decent send-off.
question: How much would the 200 dollar levy on 214 members raise?

passage: Transcript, editorial meeting, the Vale Recorder, Wednesday, deciding the front page. Editor Cho: Two candidates for Friday's front. The bypass funding confirmation, or the Ashworth farm story. Cases, one minute each. Deputy Okonkwo: Bypass. Eleven years of campaigning, 14 million dollars confirmed in writing, construction dates in hand. It touches every reader who drives, which is every reader. It is the biggest thing to happen to this town's roads since the bridge. Reporter Voss: And it is a press release. Everyone will have it, the radio had it at noon. The Ashworth story is ours alone: the farm's milk vending machine, the one the family installed as a last throw before selling up, has in eighteen months become the reason the farm survives, 400 liters a day sold at the gate, a queue on Sunday mornings, and the planning row with the district over the queue's parking is the news line. It is the whole county's argument, small farms against the rulebook, in one gateway. Cho: Photographs? Voss: Weiss shot the dawn queue this morning. Forty people and a dog in the mist. It is the best picture this paper has had all year. Okonkwo: The bypass affects thirty thousand people. Voss: The bypass will still affect them on page three. Cho: Decided. Ashworth front, Weiss's queue picture across five columns, bypass anchors page three with the full funding table, and the leader column ties them: what the town builds and what it nearly lost. Voss, eight hundred words by five. Okonkwo, get me the bypass table checked twice; the last table we ran had the roundabout figures transposed and I heard about it at the barber's for a month.
question: How many liters a day does the farm's milk vending machine sell?

passage: Verbatim minutes, Kestrel Point Surf Lifesaving Club, equipment committee. Chair Duarte: Single agenda item: the inflatable rescue boat replacement, and the quotes. Gear Officer Malloy: Both boats tested by our own crews over two weekends, same surf, same crews rotated. The Seawasp 4.2: quicker through broken water, every driver said so, and 4,000 dollars cheaper at 21,500. The Guardian 420: slower by a hair, but it self-rights from a full capsize with the kit fitted, and in February we capsized twice in training and once, as nobody here forgets, at the Gorse Beach callout. Trainer Ibsen: The crews' scorecards, since we promised to be ruled by them: Seawasp 41 points of 50, Guardian 44. The difference is entirely the capsize drill, where the Guardian scored full marks from every crew. Duarte: Motors are common to both? Malloy: Same motor, our existing spares fit either, so the decision is hull and price. Ibsen: I will say the quiet part: the 4,000 saved buys a lot of training fuel, and we are a training club before we are anything. Malloy: And I will say the quieter part: the Gorse Beach capsize took three minutes to sort with the old hull, and we had the swimmer aboard already. Three minutes in that water with a swimmer not yet aboard is the whole argument, and it does not fit on a scorecard. Duarte: The scorecards do fit it: 44 against 41. Motion: Guardian 420 at 25,500, funded 20,000 from the boat fund and the balance from the summer carnival takings. Moved Ibsen, seconded Malloy. Carried, five nil. The Seawasp agent gets a courteous letter; their boat lost to a capsize, not to a fault.
question: How many points of 50 did the Guardian score on the crews' scorecards?

passage: Transcript, joint meeting, Elmsworth Brass Band and Elmsworth Silver Band, on the amalgamation question, neutral chair from the county association. Chair Pryce: Gentlemen, ladies, one hundred and nine years of rivalry, two bands, and, by the count both secretaries certify, twenty-nine active players between you, of whom eleven play in both bands already under assumed names, a fiction everyone has enjoyed and no one believes. The question is amalgamation. Brass Secretary Howell: Our position: amalgamate, keep the brass band's name, it is four years older. Silver Secretary Nakamura: Our position: amalgamate, keep the silver name, our contest record is better: three regional titles to their one. Howell: Two of those titles used our cornets under the names I believe the chair just mentioned. Laughter. Chair Pryce: The county's proposal, which your committees asked me to bring: a new name, the Elmsworth United Band, carrying both histories; the brass band's contest registration, which is the older; the silver band's rehearsal hall, which has the parking; and the trophies of both displayed together in the hall's case, with a plaque saying, plainly, that the town could once afford two bands and now chooses one good one. Nakamura: The word chooses is doing kind work in that sentence. Howell: It is. We second it anyway. Chair Pryce: Both bands vote separately by paper tonight. Results: Brass, 13 for, 2 against. Silver, 12 for, 2 against. Carried in both bodies. First joint rehearsal is Tuesday. And the chair, who plays euphonium, asks slyly whether the united band has a vacancy. It does.
question: What name does the county's proposal give the amalgamated band?

passage: Minutes, recorded in full, Wetherfield Cheese Guild, judging protocol review after the September incident. Chair Adebayo: We all know why we are here. The September championship, the scoring tie, and what the newspaper called, with more glee than accuracy, the cheddar affair. Facts first, from the head steward. Steward Krantz: Two cheeses tied at 94 points. The rulebook's tiebreak, unchanged since 1961, says the senior judge decides. The senior judge that day, as the room knows, is married to one finalist's wholesale agent, a connection nobody had mapped until the local paper mapped it. Her decision was, in my professional view and in the view of the two other judges, correct on the cheese. The optics were indefensible anyway. Adebayo: Proposals. Krantz: Three on the table. One: blind tiebreak, both cheeses recut and rescored by all three judges, new samples, no discussion. Two: co-champions in the event of any tie, as the baking guild does. Three: the ties stand, but a declared interests register for judges, filed before the season. Ferro: Co-champions is surrender. A championship that cannot decide is a raffle. Osei: And the interests register alone would not have helped; the connection was two steps removed. Registers catch what people think to declare. Krantz: Which is why my recommendation is one and three together: blind recut for ties, register for everything else. The recut costs twenty minutes and answers all optics: nobody can lean on a cheese they cannot identify. Adebayo: Motion: blind recut tiebreak plus interests register, rulebook amended before the spring show. Moved Osei, seconded Ferro. Carried, seven to nil. And the minutes will state, for the record and for the newspaper: the cheese was good. Both cheeses were good. That was never the problem.
question: At how many points did the two cheeses tie?

passage: Transcript, site meeting, Fennimore Bog boardwalk project, volunteers and the county ecologist. Ecologist Dr. Sorel: Before anyone unloads a plank: the route changes. The orchid count came back Thursday, and the colony at marker 7 has spread eleven meters east since the survey, which is wonderful news and a routing problem, since it now sits under our planned line. Foreman Watts: How far around? Sorel: The revised line swings north for forty meters, crosses at the old peat cutting where the ground is already disturbed, and rejoins at marker 9. It adds six meters of boardwalk total. Watts: Six meters we have. The mats? Sorel: Ground protection mats the whole detour, no exceptions, and this is the part I need everyone to hear: last month a contractor on another site drove a barrow, one barrow, one trip, off the mats in a bog like this, and the ruts are there now and will be there in thirty years. Peat does not forgive. Volunteer Chen: The wood stack is at the south end. That is a long carry on mats. Watts: Chain gang, then, like the winter job. Twelve of us, planks hand to hand, nobody walks with a load. Slower and surer. Sorel: Slower by how much, honestly? Watts: We finish Thursday instead of Tuesday. Sorel: The bog has been here eight thousand years; it can spare two days. Formal bits: the revised route is staked in blue, the orchid area is taped and is a no entry zone even for photographs, and the county thanks the guild for the winter handrail work, which the otter surveyors have been using all spring, apparently. Watts: They might have said. Sorel: They are surveyors of otters, Mr. Watts. They said it to the otters. To work.
question: How much boardwalk does the revised line add in total?

passage: Verbatim record, Halberd Lane Housing Cooperative, general meeting, item six, the roof. Chair Fontaine: The survey is in. The east roof has five years left; the west roof, the one over flats 9 through 16, has two, and the surveyor's exact phrase was, do not buy a five year plan for a two year roof. Costs: west roof full renewal, 84,000 dollars. East roof, if done at the same time, 61,000, with a joint discount bringing both to 131,000 against 145,000 done separately. Treasurer Malik: Reserves stand at 96,000, built over nine years at the higher contribution rate members have grumbled about at every meeting since I introduced it. Tonight the grumbling ends, one way or the other. Voice, Mr. Herzog, flat 4: I will say it: the east roof has five years. Do the west now for 84, keep 12 in reserve, and raise the east money over four years without borrowing. Why spend on a roof that does not leak? Malik: Because the joint discount is 14,000, scaffolding is half the cost of any roof, and scaffolding goes up once instead of twice. Doing them together is cheaper by the price of a small car, and the surveyor's five years is an average, not a promise. Herzog: And if the reserve is empty and the boiler goes? Malik: The boiler fund is separate, Mr. Herzog, it has been separate since the annexe vote, you seconded the separation. Laughter. Herzog: I withdraw the boiler. The rest stands. Chair Fontaine: Motion from the treasurer: both roofs, joint contract at 131,000, reserve rebuilt at the current rate, work to start after the nesting season per the swift boxes clause in our own constitution. Vote: 19 for, 3 against, 1 abstention. Carried. And the chair notes, for the record, that the swift boxes clause has now outvoted three chairs, and long may it.
question: How much do both roofs cost under the joint contract?
